positions.text: Arpinon and Lefebvre qualify Kaal's discovery-to-confirmation design. Registered Reports fix the analysis plan before data collection. In-principle acceptance then commits the journal to publication regardless of the result, subject to Stage 2 verification that the analysis followed the Stage 1 plan. Their format also separates confirmatory analyses from later exploration and prevents conclusions from resting on ex-post exploratory results. This correspondence is limited. The article addresses a journal review format in agricultural economics. It does not verify Kaal's registered primary, the reporting of his null result, the preregistration of any exploratory signal, or the mechanical application of his confirmation rule. It also warns that preregistration alone leaves room for incomplete plans, uncertain policing, and suppression of null findings. Kaal's cycle therefore tracks recognized controls against postdiction and publication bias. Its evidentiary weight still depends on immutable registrations, disclosed deviations, and rule-bound execution.

source_provenance.sourceProposition: Arpinon and Lefebvre describe Registered Reports as a two-stage control that fixes the analysis plan before data collection, commits a journal to publication regardless of the result, verifies conformity at Stage 2, separates confirmatory analysis from later exploration, and withholds conclusions from ex-post exploratory results. They also explain that preregistration alone leaves incomplete-plan, policing, and null-result suppression risks.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Once the revision is completed, the researchers receive an In-Principle Acceptance (IPA), guaranteeing that the paper will be published regardless of the results but conditional on the authors respecting the Stage-1 analysis plan.
RRs solve both issues by guaranteeing that a result will be published regardless of the outcome and by clearly separating confirmatory analyses from exploratory analyses.

One important note is that RRs do not preclude ex-post data explorations. Rather, the results from ex-post explorations are clearly stated and no conclusions are drawn from such results, guaranteeing full transparency.
For PR however, the researchers' fidelity to the analysis and sampling plans are ultimately left to the reviewers and editors' choice of consulting the PR document, raising policing concerns.
